items.title: U.S. debt now equals the whole economy — and tax cuts since 2001 added over $10 trillion
items.summary:
Democrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy.

Clocking in at $32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living .

Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes . Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt.

The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found.

The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar , I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact . But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper , the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts.

items.title: Democrats won Congress. Now they must win back trade policy
items.summary:
Days after winning Congress, Democrats are debating whether and how to restore congressional authority over tariffs. Some in the party are focusing on reining in Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on allies like Canada, while others hope that a 2029 Democratic President might direct Trump’s expansive tariffs toward progressive priorities, such as raising labor standards. This debate is missing two things. First, it blames trade failures on Trump, when both the Trump and Biden administrations pursued similar trade policies that failed workers. Second, it focuses on taking tariff power back from the president but overlooks Congress’s role in setting trade objectives.

I have spent my career trying to make trade work for American workers. As a progressive, I urge congressional Democrats to take stock of the lessons from both the Trump and Biden administrations, which requires a course correction, even if it means restraining a future Democratic president.

Both administrations, acting unilaterally, have cost us. Congress once shared control over trade policy. Under Trade Promotion Authority (TPA), it linked its up-or-down vote on trade agreements to its negotiation objectives that included enforceable labor and environmental standards. Both administrations essentially ignored it.

items.title: Climate Advisers director: The U.S. needs a clean energy standard for AI data centers
items.summary:
Voters delivered a verdict on data centers in the midterm election. In an NBC News exit poll, 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and voters passed more than 40 local measures restricting data centers. Lawmakers now face a choice. They can answer with bans, or with rules that decide who pays for AI’s power but ignore where it comes from. Either would be half a policy. Voters want lower bills and cleaner air, and clean energy can address both. Ireland, Singapore and China have already tied data center growth to clean power. The United States should too.

Residents outside Memphis have seen the alternative. xAI has run dozens of gas turbines across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, drawing lawsuits and complaints over air quality . More are coming. Global Energy Monitor counts 189 GW of natural gas tied to data centers in development as of mid-2026, with about 17 GW already under construction . Gas appeals to AI companies because it can provide reliable, around-the-clock power, but turbine shortages and equipment backlogs could delay projects or cause them to be scrapped. This gives policymakers time to shape what will power most AI data centers in the coming years.

For now, clean energy is winning on the grid. items.title: Nvidia CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO—but the succession question remains
items.summary:
Good morning. Nvidia is the latest Fortune 500 company to name its CFO interim CEO.

The AI giant appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, replacing Jensen Huang, the company’s co-founder and longtime leader, who resigned Thursday after admitting to an affair that raised national security concerns. Kress will continue serving as finance chief while taking the helm of Nvidia.

Kress is “very much the right interim CEO,” Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner of executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates, told me. As CFO for 13 years, she knows the company’s story “front and back” and is a highly respected spokesperson with credibility among investors, Simmons said.

Nvidia’s transformation during Kress’s tenure has been extraordinary. Since she joined in 2013, revenue has grown from $4.13 billion in fiscal 2014 to $130.5 billion in fiscal 2025, while its market capitalization has climbed from about $9 billion to nearly $4 trillion today—an increase of roughly 44,000%. Kress ranks No. 49 on the Fortune 2026 Most Powerful Women list .

When I first interviewed Kress in 2022, we discussed her previous roles at Cisco, Microsoft , and Texas Instruments , as well as how Nvidia attracted and retained employees.

“I think my career background did serve me well at Nvidia,” she told me. “When I started at Nvidia, it was the smallest company that I’d ever worked for. It’s gotten quite large, but the focus is on how do you think about the future and make sure we’re ready for it to scale?”

items.title: The weaknesses that cost Binance $6.3 billion are already hitting Europe’s banks
items.summary:
When hackers drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, on October 29, it was tempting to treat it as a crypto problem. Less than a week later, Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a French lender, disclosed that hackers had made off with roughly €100 million ($112 million). 

The back-to-back attacks highlight the threat of cyber heists to traditional banks. “If a company like Binance can lose billions of dollars, the threats facing banks are overwhelming,” said Ryan Kirkley, cofounder and CEO of Global Settlement, which develops blockchain infrastructure for banks. Speaking at the Digital Asset Summit in London on November 10, he said: “It is impossible for the average bank to stay secure.” 

Binance’s founder and former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, went further. “If a crypto exchange can be hacked, banks are in a worse position, in my opinion,” he told CoinDesk days after the heist. 

The Binance hackers used a combination of social engineering and malicious software to take over crypto wallets and drain them of funds. This involved arranging a series of fake job interviews to persuade a Binance engineer to inadvertently download malware which allowed the hackers into the company’s systems. 

The FBI has seized $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency, while Binance confirmed it had “replenished” approximately 98% of the total impacted amount. 

The weaknesses hackers exploited to steal funds on Binance are not unique to crypto and the same vulnerabilities are present in traditional financial institutions, said Katerina Mitrokotsa, professor of…

items.title: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal
items.summary:
Jane Street, one of Wall Street’s leading quantitative trading firms, more than doubled its Nvidia holdings in the third quarter, according to regulatory filings released Thursday and reviewed by Fortune. The securities filings show the firm’s positions as of Sept. 30—just over six weeks before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The scandal has led Nvidia shares to fall nearly 13% over the past five days, reaching a 17-month low intraday Thursday. The regulatory disclosure, known as a 13F, doesn’t reveal exactly when Jane Street purchased the shares, or how much the firm has gained or lost on its bets though.

The market maker held 23.8 million shares worth about $5.44 billion at $228.38 at quarter end, according to the 13F. That’s over double the 11.8 million shares held, worth $2.4 billion, in the second quarter. Nvidia was its second-largest holding behind SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Jane Street declined Fortune ’s request for comment. 

The filings show what Jane Street held in late September, not what it owns now, and leave out short positions. Jane Street traders could, in theory, have shorted Nvidia after the reporting period ended and made money from the subsequent decline. The filings alone cannot tell us whether they did, though.

Options add another layer of complexity to this. The 13F also discloses that Jane Street holds a large amount of puts and calls, which are reported using the value of the underlying shares, rather than the market value of the…
items.t: Jane Street more than doubled its Nvidia stake last quarter, filings reveal

items.title: Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?
items.summary:
In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune .…
items.t: Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

items.title: A tabloid scandal bankrolled a Long Island Democrat, mostly with out-of-district money. A Hollywood-linked tycoon backed a Republican who beat him.
items.summary:
Leaked photos were supposed to end Chris Gallant’s campaign. Instead, they bankrolled it. After the New York Post published archived images of the Democrat modeling bondage gear for a San Francisco leather retailer, his fundraising took off.

In the quarter the photos surfaced, Gallant raised more than the incumbent. His October quarterly FEC report shows $929,825 in receipts for July through September. Rep. Nick LaLota reported about $609,000 for the same period.

The money bought a close loss, not a win. LaLota won a third term in New York’s 1st Congressional District last Tuesday, 51.1% to 48.9%, a margin of nearly 7,000 votes with 560 of 561 election districts reporting . Gallant first held out for absentee ballots, then conceded Wednesday . LaLota’s margin shrank from about 11 points in 2024 to about two, in a year Democrats swept to control of Congress .

Nor was the money especially local. A Fortune review of both campaigns’ raw 2026 FEC filings through Oct. 14 found that in-district donors accounted for about 16% of LaLota’s money from named individuals and just over a third of Gallant’s.

The post-leak surge followed the same pattern. In the 32 days after the Post story ran on Sept. 13, Gallant reported $276,055 in itemized contributions. Only $65,997 of it, about 24%, came from individuals inside NY-1, and almost half of that came from 62 donors in the Hamptons. Donors in Manhattan and California gave $73,606 combined, more than every donor inside NY-1 put together.
